### 1.  Reduction to an elliptic curve  

Rewrite the equation as  

\[
y^{2}=x^{3}-180 .
\]

Thus we have to determine the integral points on the elliptic curve  

\[
E:\;Y^{2}=X^{3}-180 .
\]

Clearly \(x\ge 6\) because \(5^{3}=125<180\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  Torsion part (Nagell–Lutz)

The discriminant of the curve is  

\[
\Delta =-16\cdot4\cdot 180^{2}=-2^{4}\,3^{5}\,5^{2}.
\]

If a point \(P=(x,y)\in E(\mathbb Q)\) has finite order, then by the
Nagell–Lutz theorem both \(x,y\) are integers and \(y\mid \Delta\).
Hence  

\[
y\in\{0,\pm 2^{a}3^{b}5^{c}\; :\; 0\le a\le 2,\;0\le b\le 5,\;0\le c\le 2\}.
\]

Checking these finitely many possibilities in \(y^{2}=x^{3}-180\) shows that
the only torsion point is the point at infinity \(\mathcal O\).  
Thus \(E(\mathbb Q)\) has trivial torsion.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  A rational point of infinite order  

The obvious integer solution  

\[
P=(6,6)
\]

lies on \(E\). Since the torsion subgroup is trivial, \(P\) must have
infinite order; it therefore generates the free part of \(E(\mathbb Q)\)
(i.e. \(E(\mathbb Q)\cong \mathbb Z\cdot P\)).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 4.  Multiples of \(P\)  

For a point \((x,y)\) on \(E\) the duplication formula reads  

\[
x_{2P}= \Bigl(\frac{3x^{2}}{2y}\Bigr)^{2}-2x
      =\frac{x^{4}+1440x}{4\bigl(x^{3}-180\bigr)} .
\tag{1}
\]

Applying (1) to \(P=(6,6)\) we obtain  

\[
2P=\bigl(69,-573\bigr) .
\]

Now using the addition law repeatedly one obtains the following
coordinates (written in lowest terms).

\[
\begin{array}{c|c}
n & nP=(x_n,y_n)\\ \hline
\pm1 & (6,\pm6)\\
\pm2 & (69,\pm573)\\
\pm3 & \Bigl(\dfrac{4174}{441},\;\dfrac{239338}{9261}\Bigr)\\
\pm4 & \Bigl(\dfrac{2529609}{145\,924},\dots\Bigr)\\
\vdots & \text{denominators }>1 .
\end{array}
\]

For \(n\ge3\) the denominator of the \(x\)-coordinate is larger than \(1\);
hence \(x_n\notin\mathbb Z\).  (One can prove this in general: the
denominator of \(x_{nP}\) divides \(4(x_{(n-1)P}^3-180)\) and already for

Consequently the only points of \(E(\mathbb Q)\) whose \(x\)-coordinate is
an integer are \(\pm P\) and \(\pm 2P\).
